name: Richard Coeur-de-Lion
bio: Richard I of England, king from 1189 to 1199, appears in Farnell's book among the troubadours as a maker of verse as well as a patron. Her chapter on him gives the lament he is said to have composed while a prisoner in Germany on his return from the Crusade, probably about 1193.
The verse is Ida Farnell's English version in The Lives of the Troubadours (London: David Nutt, 1896); the prose of her chapter is not reproduced here, and the Old Occitan original is not included.

poems.title: Lament Composed by Richard While Captive
poems.author: Richard Coeur-de-Lion
poems.note: Farnell's heading dates it to Richard's captivity; its closing stanza sends greeting to his sister and the Countess.
poems.text:
Never can captive make a song so fair
As he can make that has no cause for care,
Yet may he strive by song his grief to cheer.
I lack not friends, but sadly lack their gold!
Shamed are they, if unransomed I lie here,
A second Yule in hold.

My men and barons all, full well they know,
Poitevins, English, Normans, Gascons too,
That I have not one friend, however poor,
Whom I would leave in chains to save my gold,
I tell them this, but blame them not therefor:
Though I lie yet in hold.

True is the saying, as I have proved herein,
Dead men and prisoners have no friends, no kin;
But if they leave me here to save their gold,
'Tis ill for me, but worse for them, I fear,
That when I die, reproach and blame shall hear:
If I be left in hold.

Small marvel if my heart knows heaviness,
When my Lord puts my land to such distress.
If he remembered what we swore of old.
The oath we took at Sens between us twain,
I know full well that I should not remain
Many days here in hold.

Sister and Countess, God give you good cheer!
And keep my Lady, whom I love so dear;
For whom I lie in hold.
